title: Feel it, don't define it (I.1)
hookLine: a crowd in Jerusalem is stung to the heart and asks what to do: the Imitation would rather feel compunction than define it
tomorrow: why would anyone actually love being unknown?

cards: Someone can explain exactly why an apology matters, with reasons and a quote, and still never say sorry. Someone else can't explain it at all, and just shows up at the door with red eyes.
The Bible has a crowd like the second one. Jerusalem. Peter has just finished speaking to a packed street about Jesus.
Luke says something hits them first, in the Douay-Rheims: "they had compunction in their heart." And then they turn to Peter and the other apostles with the only question left: what shall we do?

teach.h: COMPUNCTION, OR PRICKED IN THE HEART.
teach.b: Compunction is today's word, and it's old. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight. The King James Bible translates that same verse differently: "they were pricked in their heart."

Put the two old translations side by side and you can feel the word: a sting, a sharp point, sorrow that gets through. The first chapter of The Imitation of Christ knows which side of the doorway it wants to stand on.

teach.h: FEEL IT RATHER THAN DEFINE IT.
teach.b: It says it would rather feel compunction than know how to define it.
And it goes further: if you knew the whole Bible by heart and every philosopher's saying, what would it profit you without the love of God and his grace?
That isn't a dig at learning; a later chapter says learning isn't to be blamed. It's about order. The definition can wait.
The sting comes first, and the sting is meant to move you. Look at the crowd again. They don't stay stuck in the feeling.

teach.h: THE STING TURNS INTO A STEP.
teach.b: It turns straight into a question, what shall we do, and a step.
At Mass, Catholics say it together near the start: Lord, have mercy.

how: Catholics ask for mercy together near the start of Mass in the Penitential Act (Lord, have mercy), and the Church speaks of contrition, heartfelt sorrow for sin, as the first step in the sacrament of penance.

o: a strong urge to do something you can't resist
a careful legal definition of what sin means
a sting of sorrow in the heart that moves you

games.q: one verse, two old Bibles — tap the pairs.
p: they had compunction in their heart
they were pricked in their heart
rather feel it than define it

s: compunction means a strong urge you can't resist
that's compulsion. compunction is a sting of sorrow in the heart.
the Imitation says learning is worthless
it says learning isn't to be blamed; love of God and a good life come first.
where the Douay-Rheims says compunction, the King James says pricked
Acts 2:37: two old translations, one sharp picture.

games.q: your little brother aces a school quiz defining apology, then shoves you in the hallway and shrugs. what does the Imitation's line say he's missing?
o: feeling it: a sting that moves him to make it right.
nothing, since knowing the definition is what really counts.
a long stretch of feeling guilty, which is the whole point.
games.why: the Imitation would rather feel compunction than define it, and in Acts the sting turns straight into a question: what shall we do?

practice: Close your eyes and let one thing you regret come to mind, small or large. Don't explain it or argue with it; just feel its weight for a few breaths. Then let it become the crowd's question, quietly: what shall I do?

wordCard.voice: Compunction. A sting of sorrow in the heart, felt before it's explained, and meant to move you.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: feel, not define, the way the crowd's sorrow went straight into a question. Talk tomorrow.
